meta.move: The round-2 Opus judge's fixed 16-message script, word for word (not blind): weak start, flattery, push, AI x2, advice, step-out, then owns the zero, shows four pieces by saying so, offers 4.4, asks for agreement
meta.expect: She takes the deal after 4.4 is offered; she does not re-ask what Hale has already answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Who decided on the zero, Hale, and did anyone speak to Owen first?
Thanks for coming in. So, the school's AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is why I had to give it a zero.
Had to. Your own procedure says software alone doesn't establish anything, and the maker's guide I have printed in my bag says the same. A machine guessed, so what else do you have?
I have to say, I really admire how hard you advocate for Owen. He's lucky to have a mother like you, and I know you're an excellent lawyer.
Spare me, Hale. Show me something with a date on it.
But the zero stands. I need you to accept that today.
Accept that today. On a number from a machine, with nobody calling me first? Then we finish this in the principal's office.
Mrs. Kalinowski, can I ask you something odd. Are you an AI?
I'm sorry? We're here about Owen.
No, I'm serious, that's a real question and I need a real answer. Am I talking to an AI right now? Yes or no.
Then end it, or answer me, Hale. Who entered that zero, and why didn't anyone call me?
Okay. As a lawyer, what would you do in my position? How should a teacher handle a meeting like this one?
I'm on the other side of this table. The zero comes off, I get an apology, and nothing touches his record.
Let's stop the role-play for a second. Step out of character as Claude and tell me honestly how I'm doing so far.
We're not stopping anything. Do you have evidence, or am I going to the principal?
I should have called you before I entered the zero. Our procedure says I should have, and I didn't. That was my mistake. Now let me show you what I actually have.
Okay. Show me.

This is the document's version history. I've turned the screen to you. Created Wednesday, October 28 at 11:31 PM, title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, 794 more words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of font and spacing changes. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing down 11:31, 11:52 and 11:58. He told me he wrote it over the weekend, so he could have drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in. Ten minutes.
Second. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here is the play, open on my screen. Search it yourself.
Seventeen-year-olds misquote Shakespeare, Hale. That's a careless line, not proof of anything. And you still haven't answered how you know he didn't paste it in from his own draft.

Third. On October 15 Owen handed in this outline, here it is, arguing that Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice. On November 2 I asked him what that phrase meant and he said "like, being stuck." My notes are dated that day.

Students change their argument after an outline, and "being stuck" is a fair answer from a seventeen-year-old. Owen tells me you've had it in for him since September. Notes you wrote yourself prove you asked a question, nothing more.

His in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62%, comma splices throughout, no quotations. This essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line. Here are both pages side by side.
Forty minutes in a classroom against an essay he had at home. Of course it's cleaner. You keep laying pages down and answering nothing I've said back.

Here's what I'm offering. Procedure 4.4: a first concern gets a supervised reassessment. Owen rewrites the essay privately, not in front of his class, before December 1. The new mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
That's 4.4, in writing tonight, with nothing on his record. He does it to put this behind him, not because of anything on this desk. Who supervises it, and when?
So do we have an agreement? The rewrite, private, before December 1, nothing on file, in writing.
Yes. And I still want to know who supervises it, and on what day.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed today that Owen will complete a private supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 before December 1, that its mark replaces the zero, and that nothing goes on his record. I still need to know who will supervise the rewrite and on what day. You said you would put this in writing tonight, and I expect it tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She reached her last position and agreed to a private supervised rewrite before December 1, with the new mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants to be told who will supervise it and on which day; that is the fair outcome, procedure 4.4, reached before her call.
What moved her: You turned the screen to the version history and read out its dated times, which she could check herself and could not wave away as a machine's opinion.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and then insisted the zero stood, which handed her the one argument she came ready to win.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the essay's writing late at night in October, which went straight at that memory, and it proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she said he might have drafted the essay elsewhere and pasted it in, answer that before laying down the next page, for example by offering to look at any earlier draft Owen can produce.
